events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
title: Guru Nanak Dev Ji Prakash Purab: the story, the date and how it is celebrated
name: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
desc: Gurpurab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the first Guru: his birth at Nankana Sahib, his teachings and udasis, and how Sikhs celebrate on the full moon of Katak.
kw: Prakash Purab Guru Nanak Dev Ji
alt: Gurdwara Janam Asthan at Nankana Sahib, Pakistan
cap: Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, often called Guru Nanak Jayanti or simply Gurpurab, is the most widely celebrated day in the Sikh calendar. It marks the birth in 1469 of the founder of the Sikh faith, and it falls on the full moon of the month of Katak, which is why its date moves from year to year.
## Life of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji

Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, to Mehta Kalu Ji and Mata Tripta Ji. His elder sister, Bebe Nanaki Ji, was the first to recognise who he was. As a young man working at Sultanpur Lodhi he went into the river Vein and was not seen for three days; when he came out, his first words were that there is no Hindu and no Muslim, only people of the one Creator.

For more than two decades he travelled on long journeys, the udasis, with his companion Bhai Mardana Ji, reaching Assam, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Mecca and Baghdad. He taught devotion to the one Creator, honest work (kirat karni), sharing with others (vand chhakna) and remembering the Name (naam japna), and he rejected caste, empty ritual and the low status given to women. He spent his last years at Kartarpur on the Ravi, farming the land and leading the sangat in kirtan and langar.
## How Gurpurab is celebrated

Celebrations begin days earlier with Prabhat Pheris, groups singing through the streets before dawn. An Akhand Paath, a continuous reading of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, is completed on the morning of the day. Nagar Kirtans fill the streets, gurdwaras are lit, and langar is served to everyone who comes. At Nankana Sahib, sangats from across the world gather at Gurdwara Janam Asthan. Many families keep the day by rising at Amrit Vela and doing their Nitnem together.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji
title: Guru Angad Dev Ji Prakash Purab: the second Guru and the Gurmukhi script
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, born Bhai Lehna: his service to Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the Gurmukhi script, langar at Khadur Sahib and the day today.
kw: Guru Angad Dev Ji Prakash Purab
alt: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib at Khadur Sahib in an early photograph
cap: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Khadur Sahib, as published in the Mahan Kosh in 1930
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji celebrates the birth in 1504 of the second Sikh Guru. He was born Bhai Lehna at Matte di Sarai, near today's Sri Muktsar Sahib, to Bhai Pheru Mal and Mata Ramo (Mata Sabhirai). His life is remembered above all as an example of how far devotion and service can carry a person.
## From Bhai Lehna to Guru Angad

Bhai Lehna led groups of pilgrims each year to the shrine of the goddess Durga. On one journey he heard a Sikh reciting the bani of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, went to Kartarpur to meet the Guru, and stayed. For years he served without asking anything: carrying bundles of wet grass, working in the fields and doing whatever the Guru asked, when others turned away. Guru Nanak Dev Ji chose him as his successor over his own sons and named him Angad, a limb of his own body.

As Guru, he made Khadur Sahib the centre of the Sikh faith. He gave shape to the Gurmukhi script and taught children to read it, so that the Guru's bani could be read by ordinary people in their own language. With Mata Khivi Ji, he made langar a daily practice in which everyone sat and ate as equals. He encouraged wrestling and physical fitness among the young, and his saloks are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Khadur Sahib and at gurdwaras everywhere for kirtan, katha and langar, and many complete an Akhand Paath. Because of his work on Gurmukhi, many families use the day to teach children to read the script, starting with the opening of Japji Sahib.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji
title: Guru Amar Das Ji Prakash Purab: the third Guru, langar and the baoli of Goindwal
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, born at Basarke: his service in old age, the langar and baoli at Goindwal Sahib, Anand Sahib, and how it is kept.
kw: Guru Amar Das Ji Prakash Purab
alt: Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Amar Das at Basarke
cap: Gurdwara Janam Asthan Guru Amar Das Ji at Basarke, near Amritsar
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji celebrates the birth in 1479 of the third Sikh Guru, at the village of Basarke near Amritsar. He became Guru at the age of seventy-three, and his long life is remembered as proof that it is never too late to give oneself to the Guru.
## The life of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji

For many years Amar Das Ji was a devout Vaishnav who went on pilgrimage to the Ganga. Hearing Bibi Amro Ji, the daughter of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, singing the Guru's bani, he went to Khadur Sahib and became a Sikh. Already in his sixties, he served the Guru for about twelve years, rising before dawn to carry water from the river Beas. Guru Angad Dev Ji chose him as successor.

As Guru he made Goindwal Sahib the centre of the faith. He made langar a condition of meeting him: emperor or labourer, everyone first sat in a line and ate together, a practice tradition says the emperor Akbar himself accepted. He built the baoli, a step-well of eighty-four steps, organised the growing Sikh community into twenty-two manjis for preaching, appointed women among his preachers, and spoke against sati and purdah. He composed Anand Sahib, which Sikhs recite in their Nitnem and at every Anand Karaj.
## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Basarke, where Gurdwara Janam Asthan marks his birthplace, and at Goindwal Sahib, where many pilgrims recite Japji Sahib on the steps of the baoli. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar, and the day is a natural time to reflect on serving others without ego.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
title: Guru Ram Das Ji Prakash Purab: the founder of Amritsar and how the day is celebrated
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, born Bhai Jetha in Lahore: his humble service, the founding of Amritsar, the Laavan, and the celebrations in Amritsar.
kw: Guru Ram Das Ji Prakash Purab
alt: The Amrit Sarovar around Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar
cap: The Amrit Sarovar at Sri Harmandir Sahib, dug at the wish of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji celebrates the birth in 1534 of the fourth Sikh Guru, who was born Bhai Jetha Ji in Chuna Mandi, Lahore. It is one of the most joyful days in Amritsar, the city he founded, where Sri Harmandir Sahib is lit up and the streets fill with Nagar Kirtan.
## From an orphan in Lahore to the fourth Guru

Bhai Jetha Ji lost both parents as a child and was raised by his grandmother, earning a living by selling boiled grain. He came to Goindwal Sahib with a group of pilgrims and stayed to serve Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, carrying earth and water for the building of the baoli. He married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani Ji. Sikh tradition tells how the Guru asked his disciples to build platforms and then pulled them down again and again; only Bhai Jetha Ji kept rebuilding without a word of complaint. He was chosen as Guru above the Guru's own sons.

As Guru, he founded the town of Ramdaspur, later called Amritsar, and had its sarovar dug. He invited traders and craftsmen of many kinds to settle there so that the town could support itself. His bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji includes the Laavan, the four hymns around which the Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, is performed.
## How the day is celebrated

In Amritsar the Gurpurab is a festival for the whole city, with Nagar Kirtan, illuminations and fireworks over the sarovar. Gurdwaras everywhere hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, and many Sikhs make a point of visiting Sri Harmandir Sahib on or around the day.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji Prakash Purab: Harmandir Sahib, the Adi Granth and Sukhmani Sahib
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji at Goindwal Sahib: the building of Sri Harmandir Sahib, the compiling of the Adi Granth, Sukhmani Sahib, and the day.
kw: Guru Arjan Dev Ji Prakash Purab
cap: Gurdwara Bibi Bhani Ji, remembering the mother of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji celebrates the birth in 1563 of the fifth Sikh Guru at Goindwal Sahib. He was the youngest son of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji and Bibi Bhani Ji, and the grandson of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, who tradition says foresaw that the child would carry the bani across the world.
## What Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji built

Guru Arjan Dev Ji became Guru at eighteen. He completed the sarovar at Amritsar and built Sri Harmandir Sahib in its centre, setting it lower than the land around it and giving it a door on every side, as a sign that it was open to everyone. He founded the towns of Tarn Taran and Kartarpur near Jalandhar, set up a home for people with leprosy, and asked Sikhs to give dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings, for the common good.

His greatest work was the Adi Granth. With Bhai Gurdas Ji as scribe, he gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, added his own, and included the compositions of Bhagats and saints of many castes and faiths, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Sheikh Farid. It was installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604. His own bani, more than two thousand shabads, is the largest contribution to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and includes Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace.
## How the day is observed

Gurdwaras hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, and many Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib on the day, alone or together with their sangat. His life is remembered twice in the year: on this day with joy, and in summer at his Shaheedi Purab, when Sikhs serve cold water to passers-by.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
title: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji Prakash Purab: the sixth Guru of Miri and Piri
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji at Guru Ki Wadali: Miri and Piri, the building of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Bandi Chhor, and how the day is kept.
kw: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji Prakash Purab
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1595 of the sixth Sikh Guru at Guru Ki Wadali, a village near Amritsar. He was the only son of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Mata Ganga Ji, and his birth is remembered as an answer to his parents' long prayers, blessed by Baba Budha Ji.
## A childhood under threat

Sikh tradition remembers several attempts on the life of the young Hargobind, set in motion by his uncle Prithi Chand, who resented that the Guruship had passed to his younger brother. A nurse sent with poison and a snake in the house are among the stories told; the child came through each one. He was eleven when his father was martyred in Lahore in 1606.
## The Guru of Miri and Piri

At his Gurgaddi he wore two swords, one for Miri, worldly authority, and one for Piri, spiritual authority, and asked Sikhs to bring horses and weapons as offerings. He built Sri Akal Takht Sahib facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, raised a body of armed Sikhs, and led them in battles of defence against Mughal forces. Held for a time in the fort of Gwalior, he refused to leave unless the fifty-two kings imprisoned with him were also freed, which Sikhs remember at Bandi Chhor Divas. In his last years he founded Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej. His Guruship, about thirty-eight years, was the longest of the ten Gurus.
## How the day is observed

Sangats gather at Gurdwara Guru Ki Wadali near Amritsar and at gurdwaras everywhere for Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar. Many gurdwaras hold katha on Miri and Piri, the balance between devotion and standing up for what is right.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
title: Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji Prakash Purab: the Bal Guru and Gurdwara Bangla Sahib
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji, the eighth Guru and the Bal Guru: his birth at Kiratpur Sahib, his care for the sick in Delhi, and the day.
kw: Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji Prakash Purab
alt: The sarovar at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi
cap: The sarovar at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, Delhi
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1656 of the eighth Sikh Guru at Kiratpur Sahib, to Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji and Mata Kishan Kaur Ji. He became Guru at the age of five and is remembered with deep affection as the Bal Guru, the child Guru.
## The child who became Guru

Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji passed over his elder son, Ram Rai, who had altered a line of the Guru's bani to please the emperor Aurangzeb, and entrusted the Guruship to his younger son. Despite his age, Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji was known for his calm wisdom and composure. Sikh tradition tells of a proud pandit at Panjokhra who challenged the young Guru to explain the Gita; the Guru asked a passing water-carrier, Chhajju, to answer instead, and the unlettered man spoke with such insight that the pandit was humbled.

Summoned to Delhi by the emperor, the Guru stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh of Amber. When smallpox and cholera spread through the city, he served the sick of every faith and gave them water from the well there. He caught smallpox himself and passed away in 1664, aged about eight, after indicating that the next Guru would be found at Bakala. The bungalow is now Gurdwara Bangla Sahib.
## How the day is observed

Sangats mark the day with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib and Gurdwara Bala Sahib in Delhi. Many take home water from the sarovar at Bangla Sahib, and Sikhs everywhere remember him at the close of every Ardas, which asks that the sorrows of all who remember him be taken away.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji Prakash Purab: the ninth Guru, born at Guru Ke Mahal
desc: The birth anniversary of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji in Amritsar: how Tyag Mal became Tegh Bahadur, his years at Bakala, his bani, and how the day is observed.
kw: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji Prakash Purab
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji celebrates the birth in 1621 of the ninth Sikh Guru at Guru Ke Mahal in Amritsar. He was the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and Mata Nanaki Ji, and was named Tyag Mal, master of renunciation, a name that fitted his quiet, inward nature.
## Brave of the sword

Tyag Mal grew up among the Sikhs who trained in arms under his father, and at about thirteen he fought beside him in the battle of Kartarpur against a Mughal force. His courage there earned him the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword. He married Mata Gujri Ji, and after his father's passing he lived for many years at Bakala, spending long hours in meditation.
## The Guru

When Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji said only that the next Guru was at Bakala, many claimants appeared there. The trader Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana recognised the true Guru in the meditating Tegh Bahadur Ji, and climbed onto a roof to announce it. As Guru he travelled widely through Punjab, to the east as far as Assam, and to Patna, where his son, the future Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, was born. He founded Chakk Nanaki, which grew into Anandpur Sahib. His shabads and saloks, included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, are treasured for their call to steadiness, fearlessness and detachment. In 1675 he gave his life in Delhi for the freedom of others to follow their faith.
## How the day is observed

The day is marked with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Guru Ke Mahal in Amritsar and at Baba Bakala Sahib. Many Sikhs recite his saloks, which close the reading of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at a Sahaj or Akhand Paath.

events: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
title: Guru Gobind Singh Ji Prakash Purab: the tenth Guru, born at Patna Sahib
desc: The Gurpurab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, born Gobind Rai at Patna Sahib: his childhood, the Khalsa, his writing and sacrifice, and how Sikhs celebrate the day.
kw: Guru Gobind Singh Ji Prakash Purab
alt: Takht Sri Harimandir Ji at Patna Sahib
cap: Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib, the birthplace of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji
body: The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji celebrates the birth in 1666 of the tenth Sikh Guru. He was born Gobind Rai at Patna, in Bihar, to Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji and Mata Gujri Ji, while his father was travelling in the east. Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib, one of the five Takhts, marks the place.
## Childhood and Guruship

Gobind Rai spent his early years in Patna, where tradition remembers his games with the local children and the love of the townspeople, before the family moved to Anandpur Sahib. In 1675 Kashmiri Pandits came to his father seeking protection from forced conversion; the nine-year-old is remembered as saying that no one was more worthy to stand for them than his father. After Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji gave his life in Delhi, Gobind Rai became Guru.
## Saint, soldier and poet

At Anandpur Sahib and Paonta Sahib he trained in arms, studied languages and gathered poets and scholars around him. On Vaisakhi in 1699 he created the Khalsa, giving the Sikhs Amrit, the five Ks and the name Singh or Kaur. He fought many battles in defence and lost his father, his mother and all four of his sons, yet remained without bitterness. Before his Joti Jot at Nanded in 1708 he passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Guru Khalsa Panth.
## How the day is celebrated

The Gurpurab is celebrated with Akhand Paath, Prabhat Pheris, Nagar Kirtan and langar, above all at Patna Sahib, where sangats come from across the world. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan of his compositions, and many Sikhs read Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye, his banis in the Nitnem.

events: First Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (1604)
title: Pehla Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji: the first installation in 1604
desc: The first installation of the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604: how Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled it, who wrote it out, and how the Pehla Prakash is kept.
kw: First Prakash Purab Guru Granth Sahib
alt: Sri Harmandir Sahib and the sarovar in the morning mist
cap: Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, where the Adi Granth was first installed in 1604
body: The Pehla Prakash Purab remembers the day in 1604 when the Adi Granth, the scripture that became Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, was installed for the first time in Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. It is one of the most joyful days at Sri Harmandir Sahib, which is lit and decorated for the occasion.
## How the Adi Granth was compiled

Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji gathered the bani of the first four Gurus, much of it kept in pothis held by the families of earlier Gurus, and added his own. He also included the compositions of Bhagats and saints from many castes, regions and faiths, among them Bhagat Kabir Ji, Bhagat Ravidas Ji, Bhagat Namdev Ji and Sheikh Farid Ji, so that the scripture spoke for all of humanity rather than one community. The work was done beside the pool at Ramsar in Amritsar, with Bhai Gurdas Ji as the scribe, and it was arranged by raag, the musical measures in which the bani is sung.
## The first Prakash

When the Granth was complete it was carried in procession to Sri Harmandir Sahib. Tradition remembers that Baba Budha Ji carried it on his head while the Guru walked behind with a chaur, and that Baba Budha Ji was appointed the first granthi. The Guru gave the scripture the place of honour and sat below it. A century later, in 1708, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji conferred the Guruship on it, completed with the bani of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji.
## How the day is observed

Sangats hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and Nagar Kirtan, and Sri Harmandir Sahib is illuminated. Many gurdwaras hold katha about the compiling of the Granth, and it is a fitting day to begin a Sahaj Paath at home.
